name: Abdominal, Pelvic, and Retroperitoneal Trauma: Damage Control Surgery

reference.source: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd ed / ATLS 10th ed
clinicalPearls: FAST examination assesses four acoustic windows: perihepatic (Morison pouch), perisplenic, pelvic, and pericardial spaces
Hemodynamically stable patients with blunt splenic or hepatic injuries are managed non-operatively with serial abdominal examinations
The Pringle maneuver compresses the hepatoduodenal ligament to arrest hepatic inflow from the hepatic artery and portal vein
Retroperitoneal hematomas are classified into Zone 1 (centromedial - mandatory exploration), Zone 2 (flank - selective), and Zone 3 (pelvic - packing)
Unstable pelvic fractures require immediate circumferential compression over the greater trochanters with a pelvic binder or sheet
reference.pathophysiology: Blunt abdominal trauma generates rapid deceleration and crush forces, injuring parenchymal organs against vertebral structures or tearing vascular pedicles. Penetrating trauma causes direct tissue laceration and blast cavitation. Uncontrolled hemorrhage, hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, and coagulopathy constitute the lethal triad of trauma. Damage control laparotomy interrupts this lethal cycle through rapid hemorrhage control, peritoneal packing, and temporary abdominal closure, deferring definitive reconstruction until physiological restoration in the surgical ICU.
additionalDifferentials: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture requiring laparotomy versus extraperitoneal rupture managed with catheter drainage
Splenic rupture with delayed subcapsular hematoma rupture versus occult mesenteric laceration
Zone 3 pelvic retroperitoneal hematoma versus active arterial internal iliac branch hemorrhage
Abdominal compartment syndrome versus severe hemorrhagic hypovolemia
additionalInvestigations: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) at bedside in the resuscitation bay
Intravenous contrast-enhanced helical CT of abdomen and pelvis in hemodynamically stable patients
Pelvic anteroposterior radiograph and chest X-ray in the primary survey
Intra-abdominal bladder pressure transduced via Foley catheter to detect abdominal compartment syndrome
